reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / NCCN & genetics references
clinicalPearls: Most commonly caused by germline variants in the succinate dehydrogenase genes (SDHB, SDHD, SDHC, SDHA, SDHAF2), with additional genes (e.g. RET, VHL, NF1, TMEM127, MAX) contributing to hereditary phaeochromocytoma-paraganglioma
Tumours arise from chromaffin tissue of the adrenal medulla (phaeochromocytoma) and from extra-adrenal sympathetic and parasympathetic paraganglia (paraganglioma)
Catecholamine-secreting tumours cause paroxysmal or sustained hypertension, palpitations, headache, and sweating, and can precipitate a life-threatening crisis
Head and neck paragangliomas are often parasympathetic and non-secretory, presenting as painless masses or with cranial nerve effects rather than catecholamine symptoms
SDHB variants carry a notably higher risk of malignant, metastatic disease, whereas SDHD-related tumours are frequently multifocal and show a parent-of-origin (paternal) inheritance pattern
Biochemical testing for catecholamine excess must precede any surgery, with appropriate perioperative preparation to prevent an intraoperative hypertensive crisis
Surveillance is lifelong and multi-site, combining biochemical screening with whole-body imaging because tumours can be multiple and recurrent
SDH-deficient tumours also predispose to gastrointestinal stromal tumours and renal cell carcinoma, broadening the surveillance requirement
reference.pathophysiology: The succinate dehydrogenase complex is a mitochondrial enzyme central to the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain. Loss-of-function variants in its subunits impair oxidative metabolism and cause accumulation of succinate, which stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor and creates a pseudohypoxic state that drives angiogenesis and proliferation in chromaffin and paraganglionic tissue. Accumulated succinate also inhibits enzymes that regulate DNA and histone methylation, producing epigenetic changes that promote tumourigenesis and, particularly with SDHB loss, malignant behaviour.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of secondary hypertension and catecholamine excess
additionalInvestigations: Germline testing of SDHx and related susceptibility genes with genetic counselling
Plasma or urinary metanephrines to detect catecholamine-secreting tumours
Anatomical imaging (MRI or CT) of the abdomen, pelvis, thorax, and head/neck
Functional imaging such as somatostatin receptor PET or MIBG for localisation and staging
SDHB immunohistochemistry on tumour tissue and screening for associated gastrointestinal stromal and renal tumours
redFlags: Unrecognised catecholamine-secreting tumour precipitating a hypertensive crisis during surgery, anaesthesia, or pregnancy
Features suggesting metastatic disease, particularly in SDHB carriers
Rapidly enlarging head and neck mass with cranial nerve involvement
New or recurrent tumours detected during surveillance of a known carrier
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies with genotype and tumour behaviour; many tumours are benign and cured by resection, but metastatic disease, most often associated with SDHB, carries a worse outlook. Lifelong surveillance improves outcomes by detecting multifocal and recurrent tumours early and enabling safe, planned surgery.
pitfalls: Operating on a suspected paraganglioma or phaeochromocytoma without excluding catecholamine secretion and providing perioperative preparation
Assuming head and neck paragangliomas are non-secretory without biochemical confirmation
Underestimating metastatic risk in SDHB carriers and providing inadequate follow-up
Neglecting the associated risks of gastrointestinal stromal tumours and renal cell carcinoma
